o: Players alternately delete any proper-length subarray (deleting a single element is always legal) until one element survives; Alice maximizes it, Bob minimizes it. For [3,7] Alice deletes 3 and wins 7. For [1,5,2] whatever Alice does, Bob removes her best candidate, leaving the second-largest, 2. Since any single-element deletion is always available, the multi-element options never beat the single-element strategy, and the game reduces to alternating deletions of extremes.
k: Deleting a length-1 subarray is always legal, so WLOG each turn deletes exactly one element: Alice always deletes the current minimum, Bob always deletes the current maximum.
With n-1 total moves, Bob makes floor((n-1)/2) max-deletions and Alice ceil((n-1)/2) min-deletions, so exactly the ceil(n/2)-th largest element survives.

a.i: Sort descending. Bob eliminates the top floor((n-1)/2) elements over the game and Alice eliminates the rest of the bottom, leaving the element at index ceil(n/2)-1 (0-based) of the descending order. Exchange arguments show neither player benefits from deviating: deleting an extreme is never worse given the opponent's optimal reply.
a.sp: O(1) extra (in-place sort) or O(n) depending on language

w: Verify the formula on tiny cases: n=2 gives the max, n=3 gives the second max, n=4 gives the second max, n=5 the third. Pitfall: off-by-one in the index; test n=2 and n=3 explicitly. Follow-up: what if Alice minimizes and Bob maximizes (symmetric, same index from the bottom), or if deletions must be contiguous blocks of length exactly m?
